title: Aisha's du'a
hookLine: O Allah, You are pardoning and love to pardon, so pardon me (Tirmidhi)

cards: "What should I say?" That's Aisha's question, and it's a practical one. The Night of Power is hidden somewhere in the last ten of Ramadan.
Suppose she happens to know which night it is. Suppose she's standing in it. Out of everything a person could ask for on a night better than a thousand months, what should she say?
She puts the question to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and the answer is short enough to learn in a minute.

teach.b: First, the source: the collection of al-Tirmidhi. Aisha asks; the Prophet tells her to say a single line. In Arabic: Allahumma innaka 'afuwwun, tuhibbul 'afwa, fa'fu 'anni.
In plain English, it calls Allah the one who pardons, says He loves to pardon, and asks Him to pardon her. That's all. Second, what it leaves out.
No list of wishes, no health, no wealth, no request about the future. On a night better than a thousand months, one request, and it's for pardon. Third, the word itself: 'afw, pardon.

Some teachers explain it as more than forgiving, wiping a thing away so that no trace is left, the way wind wipes a track off sand. The hadith doesn't spell that out. What it does spell out is the shape of the line.
It begins not with the person's need but with who Allah is, the one who pardons. Then what He loves: to pardon. Only then does it ask.
Name, then love, then the request. Fourth, how people use it.
In the last ten nights some Muslims repeat it again and again, on every odd night, in case this is the one, often quietly, in Arabic, between longer prayers.
And it travels outside Ramadan: after a hard day, or a mistake that's still stinging. One more thing belongs to Aisha. She didn't ask what the night would bring her.
She asked what she should say.

how: In the last ten nights of Ramadan, some Muslims repeat Aisha's du'a many times, in Arabic, between other prayers, and some say it at other times of the year too.

o: a one-line prayer asking the one who loves to pardon
a prayer Aisha composed for her own family alone
a long list of wishes said on the Night of Power

s: the Prophet gave Aisha a long list to recite on the Night of Power
he gave her one line, asking for pardon.
the du'a names who Allah is before it asks for anything
the one who pardons, who loves to pardon, and only then: so pardon me.
the du'a can only be said on the Night of Power
it was taught for that night, and people say it at other times too.

games.q: you're Aisha. you think you may be standing in the Night of Power. what do you do?
o: ask the Prophet what you should say.
make a list of everything you want.
wait until morning to be sure.
games.why: she asks what to say, and the answer is one line, asking the one who loves to pardon for pardon.

practice: If you pray, say Aisha's line now, slowly, in Arabic if you know it or in your own language, and then sit with it. If you don't, notice its shape instead: who is named first, what is loved, what is asked.
Then think of one thing you'd be glad to have wiped away, and just hold it.

wordCard.voice: Aisha's du'a. The line the Prophet taught Aisha for the Night of Power, asking the one who loves to pardon for pardon. Today's word.

orig.note: 'you love pardon', the heart of Aisha's du'a.

carryVoice: Your line: you love to pardon. Name, then love, and only then the request. Until tomorrow.
